plexus-lumbalis.summary: The network of nerves formed within the psoas major from the anterior rami of spinal nerves L1–L4; it supplies the lower abdominal wall, the groin and the front and inner thigh.
facts: T12 (contribution), anterior rami of L1–L4

Forms within the psoas major; its branches leave from the lateral border of the muscle (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, femoral), from its anterior surface (genitofemoral) and from its medial border (obturator)
Femoral nerve (anterior thigh muscles), obturator nerve (adductors), iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (lower abdominal wall)
Groin, anterior genital region, anterior, medial and lateral surfaces of the thigh
Iliohypogastric (L1), ilioinguinal (L1), genitofemoral (L1–L2), lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2–L3), femoral (L2–L4), obturator (L2–L4)
clinical: If the ilioinguinal nerve is injured in inguinal hernia repair, the groin and scrotum/labium majus become numb.
The cremasteric reflex tests segments L1–L2 (genitofemoral nerve).
tus: The lumbar plexus forms inside the psoas major; its branches leave from the lateral border (femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous), the medial border (obturator) and the anterior surface (genitofemoral).

n-femoralis.summary: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus; it supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the thigh (quadriceps) and gives sensation to the front of the thigh and the inner side of the leg.
facts: Lumbar plexus (posterior divisions of L2–L4)

Runs down in the groove between psoas and iliacus, passes under the inguinal ligament (muscular lacuna) into the femoral triangle and divides at once into its branches; its long sensory branch, the saphenous nerve, runs down the inner leg with the great saphenous vein
Iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, quadriceps femoris
Front of the thigh; through the saphenous nerve the medial border of the leg and foot
clinical: After injury knee extension is lost, the patellar reflex is absent and the front of the thigh is numb.
A femoral nerve block is used for pain control in hip and knee surgery.
tus: The femoral nerve enters the thigh through the muscular lacuna, lateral to the vessels; it lies outside the femoral sheath.

n-obturatorius.summary: The nerve of the muscles of the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.
facts: Lumbar plexus (anterior divisions of L2–L4)
Emerges from the medial border of the psoas, runs down along the side wall of the pelvis and passes through the obturator canal into the thigh, where it divides into anterior and posterior branches
Adductor longus, brevis and magnus (adductor part), gracilis, obturator externus
Middle of the inner surface of the thigh
clinical: Pelvic surgery or an obturator hernia can compress the nerve and cause pain on the inner thigh (Howship–Romberg sign).
tus: The ovary lies in the ovarian fossa on the side wall of the pelvis next to the obturator nerve, which explains pain referred to the inner thigh in ovarian disease.

plexus-sacralis.summary: The network of nerves formed on the posterior wall of the pelvis (in front of the piriformis) from the anterior rami of L4–S4; it supplies the buttock, back of the thigh, leg, foot and perineum.
facts: Lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) and anterior rami of S1–S4
Forms on the anterior surface of the piriformis; most branches leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen
Sciatic nerve, superior and inferior gluteal nerves, pudendal nerve, nerves to piriformis, obturator internus and quadratus femoris
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh (back of the thigh), pudendal nerve (perineum)
Superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), sciatic (L4–S3), posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh (S1–S3), pudendal (S2–S4)
tus: The sacral plexus forms on the anterior surface of the piriformis from the ventral rami of L4–S4 (including the lumbosacral trunk).

n-ischiadicus.summary: The thickest and longest nerve in the body. It supplies the muscles of the back of the thigh and all the muscles below the knee.
facts: Sacral plexus (L4–S3)

Leaves through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and runs down under the gluteus maximus between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity; it runs under the hamstrings at the back of the thigh and usually divides above the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular nerves
Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus), the hamstring part of adductor magnus; through its branches all the muscles of the leg and foot
Through its branches most of the skin of the leg and foot (except the medial border – saphenous nerve)
clinical: Sciatica: pain spreading from the buttock down the leg, usually from an L4–L5 or L5–S1 disc herniation; the straight leg raise test is positive.
Misplaced injections into the lower inner quadrant of the buttock can damage the nerve.
It can be injured in posterior dislocation of the hip.
tus: The sciatic nerve is really two nerves in one sheath: tibial and fibular parts.
In sciatic nerve injury knee flexion and all the muscles below the knee are affected; sensation of the inner thigh (obturator) and inner leg (saphenous) is preserved.

n-tibialis.summary: The larger terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it supplies the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg and all the muscles of the sole of the foot.
facts: Sciatic nerve (L4–S3)

Runs down the middle of the popliteal fossa superficial to the popliteal artery, passes under the soleus to the back of the leg and divides behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel) into the medial and lateral plantar nerves
Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus; through the plantar nerves all the muscles of the sole
The sural nerve (together with the fibular nerve) supplies the back and outer side of the leg and the lateral border of the foot; the plantar nerves supply the sole
clinical: In tarsal tunnel syndrome the sole of the foot burns and is numb.
After injury plantar flexion and toe flexion are lost and the patient cannot rise on tiptoe; the foot stays dorsiflexed and everted (pes calcaneovalgus).
The ankle (Achilles) reflex (S1) runs through this nerve.
tus: The tibial nerve is superficial in the popliteal fossa; it gives the medial root of the sural nerve.

n-fibularis-communis.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it supplies the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg. Because it winds superficially under the skin around the neck of the fibula, it is the most frequently injured nerve of the lower limb.
facts: Sciatic nerve (L4–S2)

Follows the biceps femoris tendon along the lateral edge of the popliteal fossa, winds around the neck of the fibula and divides within the fibularis longus into the superficial and deep fibular nerves

Superficial fibular nerve: fibularis longus and brevis; deep fibular nerve: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius, muscles of the dorsum of the foot
Superficial fibular nerve: anterolateral leg and most of the dorsum of the foot; deep fibular nerve: the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes
clinical: A fracture of the fibular head, a tight cast, crossing the legs or prolonged squatting causes foot drop: the foot cannot be dorsiflexed or everted, and the patient walks with a steppage gait.
tus: The common fibular nerve is the most frequently injured nerve of the lower limb (neck of the fibula).
Habitual leg crossing and tight casts are common causes of peroneal nerve palsy.

n-pudendus.summary: The main nerve of the perineum; it gives sensation to the skin of the external genitalia and perineum and motor fibres to the perineal muscles and the external sphincters.
facts: Sacral plexus (S2–S4)
Leaves through the greater sciatic foramen, winds around the ischial spine (sacrospinous ligament) and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen; it runs in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal
External anal sphincter, external urethral sphincter, perineal muscles
Skin of the perineum, external genitalia (dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris)
clinical: In childbirth a pudendal block is given near the ischial spine before an episiotomy.
Long hours of cycling can compress the pudendal nerve (pudendal neuralgia).
tus: The pudendal nerve arises from S2–S4 and gives off the inferior rectal nerve, the perineal nerve and the dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris.
In cyclists compression of the pudendal nerve in Alcock's canal can cause perineal numbness.

truncus-sympathicus.summary: A chain of interconnected sympathetic ganglia on each side of the vertebral column, from the skull base to the coccyx. It is the main distribution structure of the sympathetic nervous system, which produces the 'fight or flight' response.
facts: 3 cervical (superior, middle, cervicothoracic/stellate), 11–12 thoracic, 4–5 lumbar, 4–5 sacral; below, the single ganglion impar
From the lateral horn of spinal cord segments T1–L2 (thoracolumbar outflow); they enter the chain through the white rami communicantes
Join all the spinal nerves through the grey rami communicantes; branches also go to the head, heart and lungs
Greater (T5–T9), lesser (T10–T11) and least (T12) splanchnic nerves: to the prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, mesenteric)
sections: The pupil dilates, heart rate and contractility increase, the bronchi widen, digestion slows, the sweat glands and adrenal medulla are stimulated, and the vessels of the skin and viscera constrict.
clinical: Horner syndrome (damage to the cervical sympathetic chain – for example a Pancoast tumour): ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on the same side.
A stellate ganglion block may be used in pain syndromes of the arm.
tus: The cervical sympathetic chain has three ganglia: superior (level of C1–C4, the largest), middle (C6) and inferior (fused into the stellate ganglion).
Sympathectomy for sweating of the hands (hyperhidrosis) is done at the T2–T3 level.

systema-autonomicum.summary: The part of the nervous system that regulates the involuntary functions of the organs, vessels and glands. It consists of sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, which mostly have opposite effects, and the enteric nervous system in the wall of the gut.
facts: Thoracolumbar outflow (T1–L2); short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibres; transmitter usually noradrenaline
Craniosacral outflow (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4); long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibres; transmitter acetylcholine
Ciliary ganglion (III), pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia (VII), otic ganglion (IX)
Myenteric (Auerbach's) and submucosal (Meissner's) plexuses
Hypothalamus, autonomic centres of the brainstem
sections: 'Rest and digest': the heart slows, the pupil constricts, saliva and digestive secretions increase, gut movements speed up and the bladder contracts.
clinical: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis and bladder dysfunction.
In Hirschsprung disease there are no enteric ganglion cells in the wall of the colon.
tus: Parasympathetic ganglia lie near or inside the target organ, sympathetic ganglia close to the vertebral column (short preganglionic fibres).
All preganglionic fibres release acetylcholine (nicotinic receptors).

ganglion-spinale.summary: Mixed nerves formed where the anterior (motor) and posterior (sensory) roots from the spinal cord join in the intervertebral foramen. The ganglion on the posterior root holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons.
facts: 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
Anterior root (motor, anterior horn) and posterior root (sensory; spinal ganglion)
Anterior ramus (forms the plexuses and intercostal nerves), posterior ramus (deep back muscles and skin), meningeal branch, rami communicantes
The area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve (for example C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 front of the knee, S1 lateral border of the foot)
clinical: Radiculopathy is pain and numbness in a dermatome, weakness in a myotome and loss of a reflex caused by compression of a single nerve root.
tus: The dorsal root ganglion lies within the intervertebral foramen; it can be affected by disc herniation and foraminal stenosis.
